# Model selection

We choose the radial SVM as our final model, because it reached the highest
cross-validated accuracy (92.3%). It was also the most stable across folds (SD of 3.5 percentage points), 
and it clearly outperforms the human benchmark of 74.4%.

```{r select-model}
final_model <- models[[model_comparison$model[1]]]
cat("Selected model:", model_comparison$model[1], "\n")
```

## Important features

```{r feature-importance, code=readLines("R/visualization/importance.R"), fold="Feature importance", message=FALSE}
source("R/visualization/importance.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r}
plot_feature_importance(final_model, top = 30)
```

A majority of the most important features are taken from the mouth region. At the top are
the contrast between the upper and lower mouth (`contrast.mouth.top_bottom`). Adittionally, 
Gabor filters measuring diagonal texture across the wide mouth area seem to matter. 
These are then followed by texture features of the mouth and, to a lesser extent, the right cheek and the nose.
Interestingly, features around the eyes and brows do not appear among the 30 most important ones. 

However, it seems that for disgust different features matter.
Most mouth features matter significantly less, while the few features
that stand out are linked to the nose (`frey_slate.nose_wide.vertical.yegvx`) and to edge
directions around the mouth (`hog` features). This makes sense considering that often when
producing disgust faces, most people wrinkle their noses and can twist their mouth edges.
Important to note, because these importance scores measure how well each feature separatesthe
 emotions on its own, they show which features are informative. 
 These are not necessarily the same as the combinations of features the SVM relies on most.
